<reason>A more convincingly distinguishes necessary identification from research imposed on established recipients. B presents a serious cost—irretrievable knowledge—but never adequately explains who may override community refusal or why future descendants’ scientific interests outweigh their inheritance of meaningful community control. Its hard-stop proposal limits the intrusion without resolving that authority problem. A’s closing strengthens its case by granting unique evidence and guaranteed return, showing that its objection concerns compulsory study rather than merely indefinite delay.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s argument that a deadline limits an override without authorizing it was decisive, especially against B’s “persuasion is welcome after” formulation. B addressed serial extensions, but A showed that even one bounded study makes return conditional on accepting the research that legitimate recipients refused.</best_rebuttal>
